label: Definition 7.1
Theorem 7.1
content:
\begin{theorem}
\label{thm:7.1}
[Existence of Lebesgue measure]
There exists a $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{M}\subseteq \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ and a function $m:\mathcal{M}\to[0,+\infty]$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(Borel property)] Every open set in $\mathbb{R}^n$ belongs to $\mathcal{M}$.
\item[(Complementarity)] If $E\in\mathcal{M}$, then $\mathbb{R}^n\setminus E\in\mathcal{M}$.
\item[($\sigma$-algebra property)] If $(E_j)_{j\in J}$ is a countable family in $\mathcal{M}$, then $\bigcup_{j\in J} E_j\in\mathcal{M}$ and $\bigcap_{j\in J} E_j\in\mathcal{M}$.
\item[(Empty set)] $m(\emptyset)=0$.
\item[(Positivity)] $0\le m(E)\le +\infty$ for all $E\in\mathcal{M}$.
\item[(Countable additivity)] If $(E_j)_{j\in J}$ is a countable family of pairwise disjoint sets in $\mathcal{M}$, then
\[
 m\Bigl(\bigcup_{j\in J} E_j\Bigr)=\sum_{j\in J} m(E_j).
\]
\item[(Normalization)] $m([0,1]^n)=1$.
\item[(Translation invariance)] If $E\in\mathcal{M}$ and $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$, then $x+E\in\mathcal{M}$ and $m(x+E)=m(E)$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:thm:7.1}
Define the volume of a half-open rectangle $Q=\prod_{i=1}^n [a_i,b_i)$ by
$\operatorname{vol}(Q)=\prod_{i=1}^n (b_i-a_i)$ with the conventions $\infty-c=\infty$ for finite $c$, $\infty-\infty=0$, and $0\cdot\infty=0$. For any set $E\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$, define the outer measure
\[
\label{eq:7.u3}
m^*(E)=\inf\Bigl\{\sum_{k=1}^\infty \operatorname{vol}(Q_k): E\subseteq \bigcup_{k=1}^\infty Q_k,\ Q_k\text{ half-open rectangles}\Bigr\}.
\]
Then $m^*(\emptyset)=0$. If $E\subseteq F$, every cover of $F$ is a cover of $E$, so $m^*(E)\le m^*(F)$. For countable subadditivity, let $E_j\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\varepsilon>0$, and choose covers $E_j\subseteq\bigcup_k Q_{j,k}$ with $\sum_k\operatorname{vol}(Q_{j,k})\le m^*(E_j)+\varepsilon 2^{-j}$. Then
\[
 m^*\Bigl(\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_j\Bigr)\le \sum_{j=1}^\infty\sum_{k=1}^\infty \operatorname{vol}(Q_{j,k})\le \sum_{j=1}^\infty m^*(E_j)+\varepsilon,
\]
and letting $\varepsilon\downarrow 0$ gives countable subadditivity. Thus $m^*$ is an outer measure.

Let $\mathcal{M}$ be the family of $m^*$-measurable sets in the sense of Carath\'eodory, i.e. those $E\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ satisfying
\[
\label{eq:7.u5}
m^*(A)=m^*(A\cap E)+m^*(A\setminus E)\quad\text{for all }A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n.
\]
By the Carath\'eodory theorem, $\mathcal{M}$ is a $\sigma$-algebra, so it is closed under complements and countable unions/intersections, and the restriction $m:=m^*\vert_{\mathcal{M}}$ is countably additive. In particular $m(\emptyset)=0$ and $0\le m(E)\le+\infty$ for all $E\in\mathcal{M}$.

For a half-open rectangle $Q$, the definition gives $m^*(Q)\le \operatorname{vol}(Q)$. Conversely, any cover of $Q$ by half-open rectangles has total volume at least $\operatorname{vol}(Q)$ by finite additivity on disjoint decompositions and a standard bounded truncation argument, so $m^*(Q)\ge \operatorname{vol}(Q)$. Hence $m(Q)=\operatorname{vol}(Q)$. An open box $R=\prod_i (a_i,b_i)$ differs from $\prod_i [a_i,b_i)$ by a subset of a finite union of coordinate hyperplanes, which has outer measure $0$ (cover each hyperplane by boxes of arbitrarily small total volume). Thus $R\in\mathcal{M}$ and $m(R)=\prod_i(b_i-a_i)$; in particular $m([0,1)^n)=1$, and since $[0,1]^n\setminus[0,1)^n$ is contained in a finite union of coordinate hyperplanes, $m([0,1]^n)=1$ as well.

Every open set is a countable union of open boxes (e.g. using rational endpoints), so all open sets lie in $\mathcal{M}$; this is the Borel property.

For translation invariance, if $E\subseteq\bigcup_k Q_k$ then $E+x\subseteq\bigcup_k (Q_k+x)$ and $\operatorname{vol}(Q_k+x)=\operatorname{vol}(Q_k)$, so $m^*(E+x)\le m^*(E)$. Applying this with $-x$ gives equality, and the Carath\'eodory criterion is preserved under translations. Therefore $E\in\mathcal{M}\Rightarrow E+x\in\mathcal{M}$ and $m(E+x)=m(E)$.
\end{proof}

Lemma 7.1
Proposition 7.2
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:prop:7.2}
For $\epsilon>0$, the open box $\prod_{i=1}^n(a_i-\epsilon,b_i+\epsilon)$ covers $B$, hence
\[
\label{eq:7.u20}
m^*(B)\le \operatorname{vol}\Bigl(\prod_{i=1}^n(a_i-\epsilon,b_i+\epsilon)\Bigr)=\prod_{i=1}^n(b_i-a_i+2\epsilon).
\]
Letting $\epsilon\to0$ yields
\[
\label{eq:7.u21}
m^*(B)\le \prod_{i=1}^n(b_i-a_i).
\]
For the reverse inequality, let $(U_j)_{j\in J}$ be a countable cover of $B$ by open boxes. Since $B$ is compact, there exists a finite subset $J_0\subset J$ such that $(U_j)_{j\in J_0}$ still covers $B$. Thus it suffices to prove that for every finite cover $(U_j)_{j\in J_0}$ of $B$ by open boxes,
\[
\label{eq:7.u22}
\sum_{j\in J_0}\operatorname{vol}(U_j)\ge \prod_{i=1}^n(b_i-a_i).
\]
This is proved by induction on $n$.

For $n=1$, write $B=[a,b]$ and $U_j=(a_j,b_j)$. Let $f^{(j)}=\mathbf{1}_{(a_j,b_j)}$. Each $f^{(j)}$ is Riemann integrable on $\mathbb{R}$, and
\[
\label{eq:7.u23}
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f^{(j)}(x)\,dx=b_j-a_j.
\]
Since $J_0$ is finite,
\[
\label{eq:7.u24}
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\sum_{j\in J_0} f^{(j)}=\sum_{j\in J_0}(b_j-a_j).
\]
Because $\bigcup_{j\in J_0}(a_j,b_j)$ covers $[a,b]$, one has $\sum_{j\in J_0} f^{(j)}(x)\ge 1$ for all $x\in[a,b]$ and $\sum_{j\in J_0} f^{(j)}(x)\ge0$ for all $x$. Therefore
\[
\label{eq:7.u25}
\sum_{j\in J_0}(b_j-a_j)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\sum_{j\in J_0} f^{(j)}\ge\int_a^b 1\,dx=b-a.
\]

Assume $n>1$ and the claim holds in dimension $n-1$. Write each
\[
\label{eq:7.u26}
U_j=\prod_{i=1}^n(a_i^{(j)},b_i^{(j)})=A^{(j)}\times(a_n^{(j)},b_n^{(j)}),\qquad A^{(j)}:=\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}(a_i^{(j)},b_i^{(j)}),
\]
and write
\[
\label{eq:7.u27}
B=A\times[a_n,b_n],\qquad A:=\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}[a_i,b_i].
\]
Then
\[
\label{eq:7.u28}
\operatorname{vol}(U_j)=\operatorname{vol}_{n-1}(A^{(j)})(b_n^{(j)}-a_n^{(j)}).
\]
Define a function $f^{(j)}:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ by
\[
\label{eq:7.u29}
f^{(j)}(x_n)=\begin{cases}
\operatorname{vol}_{n-1}(A^{(j)}),&x_n\in(a_n^{(j)},b_n^{(j)}),\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
Then $f^{(j)}$ is Riemann integrable and
\[
\label{eq:7.u30}
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f^{(j)}(x_n)\,dx_n=\operatorname{vol}_{n-1}(A^{(j)})(b_n^{(j)}-a_n^{(j)})=\operatorname{vol}(U_j).
\]
Hence
\[
\label{eq:7.u31}
\sum_{j\in J_0}\operatorname{vol}(U_j)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\sum_{j\in J_0} f^{(j)}(x_n)\,dx_n.
\]
Fix $x_n\in[a_n,b_n]$. For every $x'\in A$, the point $(x',x_n)\in B$ lies in some $U_j$, so $x_n\in(a_n^{(j)},b_n^{(j)})$ and $x'\in A^{(j)}$. Thus the family
\[
\label{eq:7.u32}
\{A^{(j)}: j\in J_0,\ x_n\in(a_n^{(j)},b_n^{(j)})\}
\]
covers $A$ by open boxes in $\mathbb{R}^{n-1}$. By the inductive hypothesis,
\[
\label{eq:7.u33}
\sum_{j\in J_0: x_n\in(a_n^{(j)},b_n^{(j)})}\operatorname{vol}_{n-1}(A^{(j)})\ge \operatorname{vol}_{n-1}(A),
\]
which is equivalently
\[
\label{eq:7.u34}
\sum_{j\in J_0} f^{(j)}(x_n)\ge \operatorname{vol}_{n-1}(A)
\qquad (x_n\in[a_n,b_n]).
\]
Integrating over $[a_n,b_n]$ yields
\[
\label{eq:7.u35}
\int_{a_n}^{b_n}\sum_{j\in J_0} f^{(j)}(x_n)\,dx_n\ge \operatorname{vol}_{n-1}(A)(b_n-a_n)=\prod_{i=1}^n(b_i-a_i).
\]
Since $\sum_{j\in J_0} f^{(j)}\ge0$ on $\mathbb{R}$,
\[
\label{eq:7.u36}
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\sum_{j\in J_0} f^{(j)}\ge \int_{a_n}^{b_n}\sum_{j\in J_0} f^{(j)}\ge \prod_{i=1}^n(b_i-a_i).
\]
Therefore $\sum_{j\in J_0}\operatorname{vol}(U_j)\ge \prod_{i=1}^n(b_i-a_i)$, completing the induction. Taking the infimum over all countable covers gives $m^*(B)\ge\prod_{i=1}^n(b_i-a_i)$.

Combined with the earlier inequality, this proves $m^*(B)=\prod_{i=1}^n(b_i-a_i)$.
\end{proof}

Proposition 7.4
Proposition 7.5
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:prop:7.5}
First, $\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}\subseteq \mathbb{R}$ implies by monotonicity that $m^*(\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q})\le m^*(\mathbb{R})$. For each $N\in\mathbb{N}$, the interval $(-N,N)$ is an open cover of itself, hence $m^*((-N,N))\le 2N$. Conversely, if $(-N,N)\subseteq \bigcup_{k=1}^\infty I_k$ with open intervals $I_k$, then $[-N,N]$ is compact and is covered by the same family, so finitely many $I_{k_1},\dots,I_{k_m}$ cover $[-N,N]$. Since a finite union of intervals has total length at most the sum of their lengths and must have length at least $2N$ to cover an interval of length $2N$, it follows that $\sum_{j=1}^m |I_{k_j}|\ge 2N$, and therefore $\sum_{k=1}^\infty |I_k|\ge 2N$. Taking the infimum over all such covers gives $m^*((-N,N))\ge 2N$, hence $m^*((-N,N))=2N$.

Since $(-N,N)\setminus\mathbb{Q}\subseteq \mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$, monotonicity yields
\[
\label{eq:7.u51}
m^*(\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q})\ge m^*((-N,N)\setminus\mathbb{Q}).
\]
Also, $(-N,N)=\bigl(( -N,N)\cap\mathbb{Q}\bigr)\cup\bigl(( -N,N)\setminus\mathbb{Q}\bigr)$, so by subadditivity,
\[
\label{eq:7.u52}
2N=m^*((-N,N))\le m^*((-N,N)\cap\mathbb{Q})+m^*((-N,N)\setminus\mathbb{Q}).
\]
The set $(-N,N)\cap\mathbb{Q}$ is countable. For any $\varepsilon>0$, enumerate it as $\{q_1,q_2,\dots\}$ and cover $q_j$ by an open interval $I_j$ of length $|I_j|=\varepsilon/2^j$. Then $(-N,N)\cap\mathbb{Q}\subseteq\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty I_j$ and $\sum_{j=1}^\infty |I_j|=\varepsilon$, hence $m^*((-N,N)\cap\mathbb{Q})\le\varepsilon$. Since $\varepsilon$ is arbitrary, $m^*((-N,N)\cap\mathbb{Q})=0$. Therefore $m^*((-N,N)\setminus\mathbb{Q})\ge 2N$, and hence
\[
\label{eq:7.u53}
m^*(\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q})\ge 2N\quad\text{for all }N\in\mathbb{N}.
\]
Thus $m^*(\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q})=+\infty$.

For the second statement, $[0,1]\setminus\mathbb{Q}\subseteq [0,1]$ implies $m^*([0,1]\setminus\mathbb{Q})\le m^*([0,1])=1$ (since $[0,1]$ is an interval of length $1$). Also,
\[
\label{eq:7.u54}
[0,1]=\bigl([0,1]\cap\mathbb{Q}\bigr)\cup\bigl([0,1]\setminus\mathbb{Q}\bigr),
\]
so by subadditivity,
\[
\label{eq:7.u55}
1=m^*([0,1])\le m^*([0,1]\cap\mathbb{Q})+m^*([0,1]\setminus\mathbb{Q}).
\]
As above, $[0,1]\cap\mathbb{Q}$ is countable, hence $m^*([0,1]\cap\mathbb{Q})=0$, and therefore $m^*([0,1]\setminus\mathbb{Q})\ge 1$. Combined with the upper bound, $m^*([0,1]\setminus\mathbb{Q})=1$.
\end{proof}

label: Proposition 7.6
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:prop:7.6}
Let $S=\{(x,0):0\le x\le 1\}$. For $\varepsilon>0$, set $\delta=\varepsilon/2$ and consider the rectangle
\[
\label{eq:7.u58}
R=[0,1]\times[-\delta,\delta].
\]
Then $S\subseteq R$ and the area of $R$ is
\[
\label{eq:7.u59}
\operatorname{area}(R)=1\cdot (2\delta)=\varepsilon.
\]
By the definition of outer measure as the infimum of sums of areas of countable rectangle covers, this implies $m_2^*(S)\le \varepsilon$. Since $\varepsilon>0$ is arbitrary and $m_2^*(S)\ge 0$, it follows that $m_2^*(S)=0$.

For the $x$-axis $X=\{(x,0):x\in\mathbb{R}\}$, write
\[
\label{eq:7.u60}
X=\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty \{(x,0):-n\le x\le n\}.
\]
Each set $\{(x,0):-n\le x\le n\}$ is a translate and dilation of $S$ and can be covered by a rectangle $[-n,n]\times[-\delta,\delta]$ of area $4n\delta$, so the same argument gives $m_2^*\bigl(\{(x,0):-n\le x\le n\}\bigr)=0$ for every $n$. By countable subadditivity,
\[
\label{eq:7.u61}
m_2^*(X)\le \sum_{n=1}^\infty m_2^*\bigl(\{(x,0):-n\le x\le n\}\bigr)=0,
\]
hence $m_2^*(X)=0$.
\end{proof}

label: Proposition 7.7
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:prop:7.7}
If $m_n^*(A)=0$ or $m_m^*(B)=0$, then for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exist coverings $A\subseteq\bigcup_{i\ge1}Q_i$ and $B\subseteq\bigcup_{j\ge1}R_j$ by half-open rectangles (boxes) in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\mathbb{R}^m$, respectively, such that $\sum_i \operatorname{vol}_n(Q_i)<\varepsilon$ and $\sum_j \operatorname{vol}_m(R_j)<\infty$ (or vice versa). Then $A\times B\subseteq\bigcup_{i,j}(Q_i\times R_j)$ and
\[
\label{eq:7.u63}
\sum_{i,j}\operatorname{vol}_{n+m}(Q_i\times R_j)=\sum_{i,j}\operatorname{vol}_n(Q_i)\,\operatorname{vol}_m(R_j)=\Bigl(\sum_i\operatorname{vol}_n(Q_i)\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_j\operatorname{vol}_m(R_j)\Bigr),
\]
which can be made arbitrarily small by choosing the covering of the null outer-measure factor with total volume $<\varepsilon$. Hence $m_{n+m}^*(A\times B)=0$, and the desired inequality holds with the stated conventions. Thus assume $0<m_n^*(A)<\infty$ and $0<m_m^*(B)<\infty$; the case where one of them is $+\infty$ is immediate since the right-hand side is $+\infty$.

Fix $\varepsilon>0$. Choose coverings by half-open rectangles $A\subseteq\bigcup_{i\ge1}Q_i$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $B\subseteq\bigcup_{j\ge1}R_j$ in $\mathbb{R}^m$ such that
\[
\label{eq:7.u64}
\sum_{i\ge1}\operatorname{vol}_n(Q_i) < m_n^*(A)+\varepsilon,\qquad \sum_{j\ge1}\operatorname{vol}_m(R_j) < m_m^*(B)+\varepsilon.
\]
Then $A\times B\subseteq\bigcup_{i,j}(Q_i\times R_j)$, where each $Q_i\times R_j$ is a half-open rectangle in $\mathbb{R}^{n+m}$ and
\[
\label{eq:7.u65}
\operatorname{vol}_{n+m}(Q_i\times R_j)=\operatorname{vol}_n(Q_i)\,\operatorname{vol}_m(R_j).
\]
By the definition of outer measure,
\[
\label{eq:7.u66}
m_{n+m}^*(A\times B)\le \sum_{i,j}\operatorname{vol}_{n+m}(Q_i\times R_j)=\sum_{i,j}\operatorname{vol}_n(Q_i)\,\operatorname{vol}_m(R_j)=\Bigl(\sum_i\operatorname{vol}_n(Q_i)\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_j\operatorname{vol}_m(R_j)\Bigr).
\]
Therefore
\[
\label{eq:7.u67}
m_{n+m}^*(A\times B)\le (m_n^*(A)+\varepsilon)(m_m^*(B)+\varepsilon).
\]
Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow 0$ yields $m_{n+m}^*(A\times B)\le m_n^*(A)m_m^*(B)$.
\end{proof}

label: Proposition 7.8
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:prop:7.8}
Set $A=\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty A_j$ and define measurable sets
\[
\label{eq:7.u69}
B_1:=A_1,\qquad B_j:=A_j\setminus A_{j-1}\quad (j\ge 2).
\]
Then the sets $(B_j)_{j\ge 1}$ are pairwise disjoint and, for each $N\ge 1$,
\[
\label{eq:7.u70}
A_N=\bigcup_{j=1}^N B_j,\qquad A=\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty B_j.
\]
By finite additivity of Lebesgue measure on disjoint measurable sets,
\[
\label{eq:7.u71}
m(A_N)=\sum_{j=1}^N m(B_j)\quad (N\ge 1).
\]
By countable additivity on disjoint measurable sets,
\[
\label{eq:7.u72}
m(A)=\sum_{j=1}^\infty m(B_j).
\]
Since the partial sums $\sum_{j=1}^N m(B_j)$ increase to $\sum_{j=1}^\infty m(B_j)$, it follows that
\[
\label{eq:7.u73}
\lim_{N\to\infty} m(A_N)=\lim_{N\to\infty}\sum_{j=1}^N m(B_j)=\sum_{j=1}^\infty m(B_j)=m(A).
\]
\end{proof}

label: Proposition 7.9
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:prop:7.9}
Set $A:=\bigcap_{j=1}^\infty A_j$ and define $B_j:=A_1\setminus A_j$ for $j\ge 1$. Then $(B_j)_{j\ge 1}$ is an increasing sequence of measurable sets and
\[
\label{eq:7.u75}
\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty B_j 
= \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty (A_1\setminus A_j)
= A_1\setminus \bigcap_{j=1}^\infty A_j
= A_1\setminus A.
\]
By countable additivity applied to the disjoint union $A_1 = A_j \sqcup B_j$,
\[
\label{eq:7.u76}
m(A_1)=m(A_j)+m(B_j)\quad\text{for all }j\ge 1.
\]
Since $(B_j)$ increases, continuity from below yields
\[
\label{eq:7.u77}
\lim_{j\to\infty} m(B_j)= m\Bigl(\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty B_j\Bigr)=m(A_1\setminus A).
\]
Taking limits in $m(A_j)=m(A_1)-m(B_j)$ gives
\[
\label{eq:7.u78}
\lim_{j\to\infty} m(A_j)= m(A_1)-m(A_1\setminus A).
\]
Because $A\subseteq A_1$ and $m(A_1)<\infty$, countable additivity for the disjoint union $A_1 = A \sqcup (A_1\setminus A)$ implies
\[
\label{eq:7.u79}
m(A_1)=m(A)+m(A_1\setminus A),
\]
so $m(A_1)-m(A_1\setminus A)=m(A)$. Therefore $\lim_{j\to\infty} m(A_j)=m(A)$, as required.
\end{proof}

label: Proposition 7.10
Proposition 7.11
Proposition 7.12
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:prop:7.12}
Let $\mathbf{Q}$ be the set of rational numbers. For $x\in\mathbf{R}$ write $x+\mathbf{Q}:=\{x+q:q\in\mathbf{Q}\}$, and call such a set a coset of $\mathbf{Q}$. If $(x+\mathbf{Q})\cap(y+\mathbf{Q})\neq\emptyset$, then $x+q=y+q'$ for some $q,q'\in\mathbf{Q}$, hence $x-y=q'-q\in\mathbf{Q}$ and therefore $x+\mathbf{Q}=y+\mathbf{Q}$. Thus any two cosets are either equal or disjoint.

Every coset $x+\mathbf{Q}$ meets $[0,1]$: since $\mathbf{Q}$ is dense in $\mathbf{R}$, the interval $[-x,1-x]$ contains some $q\in\mathbf{Q}$, and then $x+q\in(x+\mathbf{Q})\cap[0,1]$.

Let $\mathbf{R}/\mathbf{Q}$ denote the set of all cosets of $\mathbf{Q}$. Using the axiom of choice, select for each coset $A\in\mathbf{R}/\mathbf{Q}$ a point $x_A\in A\cap[0,1]$, and define
\[
\label{eq:7.u91}
E:=\{x_A: A\in\mathbf{R}/\mathbf{Q}\}\subseteq[0,1].
\]
Set $J:=\mathbf{Q}\cap[-1,1]$ and
\[
\label{eq:7.u92}
X:=\bigcup_{q\in J} (q+E).
\]
Then $X\subseteq[-1,2]$ because $E\subseteq[0,1]$ and $q\in[-1,1]$. Moreover $[0,1]\subseteq X$: given $y\in[0,1]$, let $A:=y+\mathbf{Q}$. Then $x_A\in A$, so $y-x_A\in\mathbf{Q}$. Since $y,x_A\in[0,1]$, one has $q:=y-x_A\in[-1,1]$, so $q\in J$ and $y=q+x_A\in q+E\subseteq X$.

The family $(q+E)_{q\in J}$ is pairwise disjoint. Indeed, if $(q+E)\cap(q'+E)\neq\emptyset$, then there exist cosets $A,A'\in\mathbf{R}/\mathbf{Q}$ such that $q+x_A=q'+x_{A'}$. Hence $x_A-x_{A'}\in\mathbf{Q}$, so $x_A+\mathbf{Q}=x_{A'}+\mathbf{Q}$, i.e. $A=A'$. By construction, each coset has exactly one chosen representative in $E$, so $x_A=x_{A'}$, and therefore $q=q'$.

Since $[0,1]\subseteq X\subseteq[-1,2]$, monotonicity of $m^*$ and the normalization $m^*([a,b])=b-a$ yield
\[
\label{eq:7.u93}
1=m^*([0,1])\le m^*(X)\le m^*([-1,2])=3.
\]
By translation invariance of $m^*$,
\[
\label{eq:7.u94}
\sum_{q\in J} m^*(q+E)=\sum_{q\in J} m^*(E).
\]
The set $J$ is countably infinite. If $m^*(E)=0$, then $\sum_{q\in J} m^*(E)=0$. If $m^*(E)>0$, then for each $N\in\mathbf{N}$ one can choose distinct $q_1,\dots,q_N\in J$ and obtain
\[
\label{eq:7.u95}
\sum_{q\in J} m^*(E)\ge \sum_{k=1}^N m^*(E)=N\,m^*(E),
\]
so $\sum_{q\in J} m^*(E)=+\infty$. In either case,
\[
\label{eq:7.u96}
\sum_{q\in J} m^*(q+E)\notin[1,3].
\]
Since $m^*(X)\in[1,3]$, it follows that
\[
\label{eq:7.u97}
m^*(X)\neq \sum_{q\in J} m^*(q+E).
\]
Finally, define $A_q:=q+E$ for $q\in J$. Then $(A_q)_{q\in J}$ is a countable family of pairwise disjoint subsets of $\mathbf{R}$ and $\bigcup_{q\in J}A_q=X$, so the required inequality holds.
\end{proof}

label: Proposition 7.13
Definition 7.5
Lemma 7.2
Lemma 7.3
Lemma 7.4
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:lem:7.4}
Since $J$ is finite, write $J=\{1,\dots,n\}$ and set $F_k:=\bigcup_{j=1}^k E_j$ for $k=1,\dots,n$.

Fix $A\subseteq X$. The inequality
\[
\label{eq:7.u103}
m^*(A\cap F_n)\le\sum_{j=1}^n m^*(A\cap E_j)
\]
follows from the countable subadditivity of $m^*$ applied to the family $(A\cap E_j)_{j=1}^n$.

For the reverse inequality, use induction on $n$. For $n=1$ the identity is trivial. Assume the identity holds for $n-1$. Since $F_{n-1}$ is $m^*$-measurable (finite unions of $m^*$-measurable sets are $m^*$-measurable) and $E_n$ is $m^*$-measurable, and $F_{n-1}\cap E_n=\varnothing$, the Carath\'eodory measurability condition for the measurable set $E_n$ applied to the set $A\cap(F_{n-1}\cup E_n)$ yields
\[
\label{eq:7.u104}
m^*\bigl(A\cap(F_{n-1}\cup E_n)\bigr)=m^*\bigl(A\cap(F_{n-1}\cup E_n)\cap E_n\bigr)+m^*\bigl(A\cap(F_{n-1}\cup E_n)\cap E_n^c\bigr).
\]
Because $F_{n-1}\subseteq E_n^c$ and $E_n\subseteq F_{n-1}^c$, this becomes
\[
\label{eq:7.u105}
m^*\bigl(A\cap(F_{n-1}\cup E_n)\bigr)=m^*(A\cap E_n)+m^*(A\cap F_{n-1}).
\]
By the induction hypothesis, $m^*(A\cap F_{n-1})=\sum_{j=1}^{n-1} m^*(A\cap E_j)$, hence
\[
\label{eq:7.u106}
m^*(A\cap F_n)=\sum_{j=1}^{n} m^*(A\cap E_j).
\]
This completes the induction and proves the first claimed identity.

Taking $A=X$ gives
\[
\label{eq:7.u107}
m^*\Bigl(\bigcup_{j=1}^n E_j\Bigr)=\sum_{j=1}^n m^*(E_j).
\]
Since each $E_j$ and $\bigcup_{j=1}^n E_j$ are $m^*$-measurable, $m$ agrees with $m^*$ on these sets, so
\[
\label{eq:7.u108}
m\Bigl(\bigcup_{j\in J}E_j\Bigr)=\sum_{j\in J} m(E_j).
\]
\end{proof}

label: Proposition 7.14
Lemma 7.5
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:lem:7.5}
Write $E:=\bigcup_{j\in J}E_j$.

\emph{Measurability of $E$.} Since $J$ is countable, fix an enumeration $J=\{j_1,j_2,\dots\}$ and define $F_N:=\bigcup_{k=1}^N E_{j_k}$. Let $A\subseteq X$ be arbitrary. Then
\[
\label{eq:7.u113}
A\cap E=\bigcup_{k=1}^\infty (A\cap E_{j_k}),
\]
and by countable subadditivity,
\[
\label{eq:7.u114}
m^*(A\cap E)\le \sum_{k=1}^\infty m^*(A\cap E_{j_k})=\sup_{N\ge 1}\sum_{k=1}^N m^*(A\cap E_{j_k}).
\]
The sets $(A\cap E_{j_k})_{k=1}^N$ are disjoint and their union is $A\cap F_N$, hence by finite additivity of $m^*$ on disjoint measurable sets,
\[
\label{eq:7.u115}
\sum_{k=1}^N m^*(A\cap E_{j_k})=m^*(A\cap F_N).
\]
Therefore
\[
\label{eq:7.u116}
m^*(A\cap E)\le \sup_{N\ge 1} m^*(A\cap F_N).
\]
Since $F_N\subseteq E$, one has $A\setminus E\subseteq A\setminus F_N$, and by monotonicity,
\[
\label{eq:7.u117}
m^*(A\setminus E)\le m^*(A\setminus F_N)\qquad (N\ge 1).
\]
Combining,
\[
\label{eq:7.u118}
m^*(A\cap E)+m^*(A\setminus E)
\le \sup_{N\ge 1}\bigl(m^*(A\cap F_N)+m^*(A\setminus F_N)\bigr).
\]
Each $F_N$ is measurable (finite union of measurable sets), so by the Carath\'eodory criterion,
\[
\label{eq:7.u119}
m^*(A\cap F_N)+m^*(A\setminus F_N)=m^*(A)\qquad (N\ge 1).
\]
Hence $m^*(A\cap E)+m^*(A\setminus E)\le m^*(A)$. The reverse inequality $m^*(A)\le m^*(A\cap E)+m^*(A\setminus E)$ follows from subadditivity and the decomposition $A=(A\cap E)\cup (A\setminus E)$ into disjoint sets. Therefore $m^*(A)=m^*(A\cap E)+m^*(A\setminus E)$ for all $A$, so $E$ is $m^*$-measurable.

\emph{Additivity.} For each $N$, finite additivity on disjoint measurable sets gives
\[
\label{eq:7.u120}
m(F_N)=\sum_{k=1}^N m(E_{j_k}).
\]
Moreover $F_N\subseteq E$, so $m(F_N)\le m(E)$ for all $N$, and thus
\[
\label{eq:7.u121}
\sum_{k=1}^\infty m(E_{j_k})=\sup_{N\ge 1} m(F_N)\le m(E).
\]
For the reverse inequality, for each $N$ the set $E\setminus F_N=\bigcup_{k>N}E_{j_k}$ is measurable and disjoint from $F_N$, hence
\[
\label{eq:7.u122}
m(E)=m(F_N)+m(E\setminus F_N)\ge m(F_N).
\]
Taking the supremum over $N$ yields $m(E)\ge \sup_{N\ge 1} m(F_N)=\sum_{k=1}^\infty m(E_{j_k})$. Combining both inequalities gives
\[
\label{eq:7.u123}
m(E)=\sum_{k=1}^\infty m(E_{j_k}),
\]
which is independent of the chosen enumeration of $J$.
\end{proof}

label: Lemma 7.6
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:lem:7.6}
Let $E:=\bigcup_{j\in J} E_j$. To show that $E$ is $m^*$-measurable, fix any $A\subseteq X$. By countable subadditivity we have
\[
\label{eq:7.u125}
m^*(A)\le m^*(A\cap E)+m^*(A\setminus E).
\]
Enumerate $J=\{j_1,j_2,\dots\}$ and set $F_N:=\bigcup_{k=1}^N E_{j_k}$. Then $A\cap E=\bigcup_{k\ge 1}(A\cap E_{j_k})$, so
\[
\label{eq:7.u126}
m^*(A\cap E)\le \sup_{N\ge 1} m^*(A\cap F_N).
\]
Since $F_N\subseteq E$, we have $A\setminus E\subseteq A\setminus F_N$ and thus
\[
\label{eq:7.u127}
m^*(A\setminus E)\le m^*(A\setminus F_N)
\]
for all $N$. Because each $F_N$ is measurable (finite union of measurable sets),
\[
\label{eq:7.u128}
m^*(A)=m^*(A\cap F_N)+m^*(A\setminus F_N).
\]
Taking the supremum over $N$ yields $m^*(A)\ge m^*(A\cap E)+m^*(A\setminus E)$. Together with \eqref{eq:7.u125} this gives equality, so $E$ is $m^*$-measurable.

For the additivity of $m$, enumerate $J=\{j_1,j_2,\dots\}$ and let $F_N$ be as above. By countable subadditivity,
\[
\label{eq:7.u129}
m(E)\le \sum_{j\in J} m(E_j)=\sum_{k=1}^\infty m(E_{j_k}).
\]
On the other hand, by finite additivity and monotonicity,
\[
\label{eq:7.u130}
m(E)\ge m(F_N)=\sum_{k=1}^N m(E_{j_k})
\]
for all $N$, hence $m(E)\ge \sum_{k=1}^\infty m(E_{j_k})$. Therefore
\[
\label{eq:7.u131}
m(E)=\sum_{j\in J} m(E_j).
\]
\end{proof}

label: Lemma 7.7
Lemma 7.8
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:lem:7.8}
Call an open box $B=\prod_{i=1}^n(a_i,b_i)$ \emph{rational} if all endpoints $a_i,b_i$ are rational. The set of all rational boxes is countable since each such box is determined by a point of $\mathbb{Q}^{2n}$.

Claim: for any open ball $B(x,r)\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ there exists a rational box $B$ such that $x\in B\subset B(x,r)$. Write $x=(x_1,\dots,x_n)$. For each $1\le i\le n$, choose rationals $a_i,b_i$ with
\[
\label{eq:7.u133}
x_i-\frac{r}{n}<a_i<x_i<b_i<x_i+\frac{r}{n}.
\]
Then $B:=\prod_{i=1}^n(a_i,b_i)$ is a rational box and $x\in B$. If $y\in B$, then $|y_i-x_i|<r/n$ for all $i$, hence
\[
\label{eq:7.u134}
\|y-x\|\le \sum_{i=1}^n |y_i-x_i|<\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{r}{n}=r,
\]
so $y\in B(x,r)$ and therefore $B\subset B(x,r)$.

Let $\Sigma$ be the set of all rational boxes $B$ such that $B\subset E$. Then $\bigcup_{B\in\Sigma}B\subset E$ is immediate. Conversely, if $x\in E$, then since $E$ is open there exists $r>0$ such that $B(x,r)\subset E$. By the claim, there exists a rational box $B$ with $x\in B\subset B(x,r)\subset E$, so $B\in\Sigma$ and $x\in\bigcup_{B\in\Sigma}B$. Hence $E=\bigcup_{B\in\Sigma}B$.

Since $\Sigma$ is a subset of the countable set of all rational boxes, $\Sigma$ is finite or countable. 
\end{proof}

label: Lemma 7.9
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:lem:7.9}
It suffices to prove the statement for open sets, since if $F\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ is closed then $F^c$ is open, and the complement of a Lebesgue measurable set is Lebesgue measurable.

Let $E\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be open. For each $x\in E$ choose $r_x>0$ such that the open ball $B(x,r_x)\subseteq E$. Let $\mathcal{B}$ be the collection of all open boxes
\[
\label{eq:7.u135}
Q(a,b)=\prod_{i=1}^n (a_i,b_i)
\]
with rational endpoints $a_i,b_i\in\mathbb{Q}$ such that $\overline{Q(a,b)}\subseteq E$. Since the set of such rational boxes is countable, $\mathcal{B}$ is countable.

The union of $\mathcal{B}$ equals $E$. Indeed, fix $x\in E$ and choose $r=r_x$ with $B(x,r)\subseteq E$. Choose $\rho\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $0<\rho<r/\sqrt{n}$. For each $i$ choose rationals $a_i,b_i$ with
\[
\label{eq:7.u136}
x_i-\rho<a_i<x_i<b_i<x_i+\rho.
\]
Then $x\in Q(a,b)$ and $Q(a,b)\subseteq \prod_{i=1}^n (x_i-\rho,x_i+\rho)\subseteq B(x,r)\subseteq E$, hence also $\overline{Q(a,b)}\subseteq \overline{B(x,r)}\subseteq E$ because $E$ is open. Thus $Q(a,b)\in\mathcal{B}$ and $x$ belongs to the union of $\mathcal{B}$. Since $x\in E$ was arbitrary, $E=\bigcup_{Q\in\mathcal{B}} Q$.

Each open box is Lebesgue measurable, and a countable union of Lebesgue measurable sets is Lebesgue measurable. Therefore $E$ is Lebesgue measurable. Consequently every closed set is also Lebesgue measurable.
\end{proof}

label: Proposition 7.15
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:prop:7.15}
Since $B$ is Lebesgue measurable, for every $E\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ the Lebesgue measure $m$ satisfies Carath\'eodory's criterion
\[
\label{eq:7.u137}
m(E)=m(E\cap B)+m(E\setminus B).
\]
Fix any $E\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$. Because $A\subseteq B$, one has $E\cap A\subseteq E\cap B$ and $E\setminus B\subseteq E\setminus A$. Hence, by monotonicity,
\[
\label{eq:7.u138}
m(E\cap A)\le m(E\cap B),\qquad m(E\setminus B)\le m(E\setminus A).
\]
Using $m(E\cap B)\le m(B)=0$, it follows that $m(E\cap A)=0$. Therefore
\[
\label{eq:7.u139}
m(E)=m(E\cap B)+m(E\setminus B)=0+m(E\setminus B)=m(E\setminus B)\le m(E\setminus A).
\]
On the other hand, $E\setminus A\subseteq E$ implies $m(E\setminus A)\le m(E)$. Consequently $m(E)=m(E\setminus A)$. Since $m(E\cap A)=0$, this yields
\[
\label{eq:7.u140}
m(E)=m(E\cap A)+m(E\setminus A),
\]
for every $E\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, so $A$ is Lebesgue measurable.

Taking $E=A$ gives $m(A)=m(A\cap A)+m(A\setminus A)=m(A)+0$, and also $m(A)\le m(B)=0$ by monotonicity; thus $m(A)=0$.
\end{proof}

label: Proposition 7.16
Definition 7.6
Lemma 7.10
Lemma 7.11
Theorem 7.3
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:thm:7.3}
Assume first that \(f\) is measurable. For each \(j\in\{1,\dots,m\}\), let \(\pi_j:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}\) be the coordinate projection \(\pi_j(y_1,\dots,y_m)=y_j\). For any \(a\in\mathbb{R}\), the set \(\pi_j^{-1}(( -\infty,a)) = \mathbb{R}\times\cdots\times\mathbb{R}\times( -\infty,a)\times\mathbb{R}\times\cdots\times\mathbb{R}\) is an open subset of \(\mathbb{R}^m\), hence Borel measurable. Since \(f\) is measurable,
\[
\label{eq:7.u147}
\{x\in\Omega: f_j(x)<a\}=\{x\in\Omega: \pi_j(f(x))<a\}=f^{-1}\bigl(\pi_j^{-1}(( -\infty,a))\bigr)
\]
is measurable in \(\Omega\). Therefore each \(f_j\) is measurable.

Conversely, assume each \(f_j\) is measurable. For \(a=(a_1,\dots,a_m)\in\mathbb{R}^m\), define the open rectangle
\[
\label{eq:7.u148}
R(a):=( -\infty,a_1)\times\cdots\times( -\infty,a_m)\subset\mathbb{R}^m.
\]
Then
\[
\label{eq:7.u149}
f^{-1}(R(a))=\bigcap_{j=1}^m \{x\in\Omega: f_j(x)<a_j\},
\]
which is measurable as a finite intersection of measurable sets. Let
\[
\label{eq:7.u150}
\mathcal{G}:=\{E\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m: f^{-1}(E)\text{ is measurable in }\Omega\}.
\]
Then \(\mathcal{G}\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\mathbb{R}^m\). The family \(\mathcal{R}:=\{R(a): a\in\mathbb{R}^m\}\) is closed under finite intersections and generates the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^m)\), since \(\{(b_1,c_1)\times\cdots\times(b_m,c_m): b_j<c_j\}\) consists of finite intersections of sets of the form \(R(a)\) and complements thereof, and these open rectangles form a basis for the topology of \(\mathbb{R}^m\). As \(\mathcal{R}\subseteq\mathcal{G}\) and \(\mathcal{G}\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra, it follows that \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^m)\subseteq\mathcal{G}\). Hence for every Borel set \(E\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\), the preimage \(f^{-1}(E)\) is measurable in \(\Omega\), i.e. \(f\) is measurable.
\end{proof}

label: Lemma 7.12
Theorem 7.4
Theorem 7.5
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:thm:7.5}
Define $h:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^2$ by $h(x)=(f(x),g(x))$. Since $f$ and $g$ are measurable, for any Borel sets $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$,
\[
\label{eq:7.u153}
h^{-1}(A\times B)=f^{-1}(A)\cap g^{-1}(B)
\]
is measurable in $\Omega$, hence $h$ is measurable.

Let $k:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}$ be continuous. Then for any Borel set $E\subseteq\mathbb{R}$, $k^{-1}(E)$ is Borel in $\mathbb{R}^2$, and therefore
\[
\label{eq:7.u154}
(k\circ h)^{-1}(E)=h^{-1}\bigl(k^{-1}(E)\bigr)
\]
is measurable in $\Omega$. Hence $k\circ h$ is measurable.

Applying this with the continuous maps
\[
\label{eq:7.u155}
(a,b)\mapsto a+b,\quad (a,b)\mapsto a-b,\quad (a,b)\mapsto ab,\quad (a,b)\mapsto \max\{a,b\},\quad (a,b)\mapsto \min\{a,b\},
\]
shows that $f+g$, $f-g$, $fg$, $\max(f,g)$, and $\min(f,g)$ are measurable.

If $g(x)\neq 0$ for all $x\in\Omega$, then $h(\Omega)\subseteq U:=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb{R}^2:b\neq 0\}$. The map $k:U\to\mathbb{R}$ given by $k(a,b)=a/b$ is continuous, and $U$ is Borel in $\mathbb{R}^2$; extending $k$ to a Borel measurable map on $\mathbb{R}^2$ (for instance by defining it arbitrarily on $\mathbb{R}^2\setminus U$) shows that $k\circ h=f/g$ is measurable on $\Omega$.
\end{proof}

label: Lemma 7.13
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:lem:7.13}
Assume first that \(f\) is measurable. Since \((a,\infty)\) is an open subset of \(\mathbb{R}\), measurability of \(f\) implies that \(f^{-1}((a,\infty))\) is measurable in \(\Omega\) for every \(a\in\mathbb{R}\).

Conversely, assume that \(f^{-1}((a,\infty))\) is measurable in \(\Omega\) for every \(a\in\mathbb{R}\). Define
\[
\label{eq:7.u156}
\mathcal{G}:=\{E\subseteq\mathbb{R}: f^{-1}(E)\text{ is measurable in }\Omega\}.
\]
Then \(\mathcal{G}\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\mathbb{R}\): \(\mathbb{R}\in\mathcal{G}\) since \(f^{-1}(\mathbb{R})=\Omega\) is measurable; if \(E\in\mathcal{G}\), then \(f^{-1}(E^c)=\Omega\setminus f^{-1}(E)\) is measurable, so \(E^c\in\mathcal{G}\); and if \((E_k)_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\subseteq\mathcal{G}\), then
\[
\label{eq:7.u157}
f^{-1}\Big(\bigcup_{k=1}^\infty E_k\Big)=\bigcup_{k=1}^\infty f^{-1}(E_k)
\]
is measurable, so \(\bigcup_{k}E_k\in\mathcal{G}\).

By assumption, \((a,\infty)\in\mathcal{G}\) for every \(a\in\mathbb{R}\). Hence for each \(a\in\mathbb{R}\),
\[
\label{eq:7.u158}
(-\infty,a)=\bigcup_{m=1}^\infty \big(-\infty, a-\tfrac1m\big)=\bigcup_{m=1}^\infty \big( a-\tfrac1m,\infty\big)^c
\]
belongs to \(\mathcal{G}\), and therefore
\[
\label{eq:7.u159}
(a,b)=(-\infty,b)\cap(a,\infty)\in\mathcal{G}\qquad(a<b).
\]
Thus \(\mathcal{G}\) contains all open intervals, and since \(\mathcal{G}\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra, it contains the \(\sigma\)-algebra generated by open intervals, i.e. the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\mathbb{R}\). Therefore \(f^{-1}(U)\) is measurable in \(\Omega\) for every open set \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}\), which is equivalent to \(f\) being measurable.
\end{proof}

label: Definition 7.7
Lemma 7.14
proof:
\begin{proof}
\label{prf:lem:7.14}
Let $g:=\sup_{n\ge 1} f_n$. For any $a\in\mathbb{R}$,
\[
\label{eq:7.u163}
\{x\in\Omega: g(x)>a\}=\bigcup_{n\ge 1}\{x\in\Omega: f_n(x)>a\}=\bigcup_{n\ge 1} f_n^{-1}((a,+\infty]).
\]
Each set $f_n^{-1}((a,+\infty])$ is measurable because $f_n$ is measurable, and a countable union of measurable sets is measurable; hence $g$ is measurable.

Let $h:=\inf_{n\ge 1} f_n$. For any $a\in\mathbb{R}$,
\[
\label{eq:7.u164}
\{x\in\Omega: h(x)<a\}=\bigcup_{n\ge 1}\{x\in\Omega: f_n(x)<a\}=\bigcup_{n\ge 1} f_n^{-1}([ -\infty, a)).
\]
Thus $h$ is measurable.

For each $N\ge 1$, the functions $x\mapsto \sup_{n\ge N} f_n(x)$ and $x\mapsto \inf_{n\ge N} f_n(x)$ are measurable by the previous two parts applied to the tails $(f_n)_{n\ge N}$. Using the pointwise identities
\[
\label{eq:7.u165}
\limsup_{n\to\infty} f_n = \inf_{N\ge 1}\, \sup_{n\ge N} f_n,
\qquad
\liminf_{n\to\infty} f_n = \sup_{N\ge 1}\, \inf_{n\ge N} f_n,
\]
$\limsup_{n\to\infty} f_n$ is a countable infimum of measurable functions and $\liminf_{n\to\infty} f_n$ is a countable supremum of measurable functions, hence both are measurable.

If $f_n\to f$ pointwise, then for each $x\in\Omega$ one has $f(x)=\limsup_{n\to\infty} f_n(x)=\liminf_{n\to\infty} f_n(x)$, so $f$ is measurable.
\end{proof}

label: Proposition 7.17
